Related articles Features Feb 23, 2026 The making of Claude Code View more At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research. Claude is able to autonomously iterate on research loops, micro-optimize complex programs, and build new services from the ground up at a speed and scale we haven’t seen before. The bottleneck, now, is all of the developer infrastructure built for human scale: source control, builds, and CI. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce. Changes merged to our monorepo per day, from January to September 2026. In order to support this growth, we built Scion, an in-house version control system, and fully migrated our monorepo from git in five months. We also built and shipped a code review surface (called Antique), code search, a rich source control IAM system, novel ways of managing and landing large amounts of reviewed code, and more, all in that same time period. In this post, we’ll focus on how we built Scion specifically. It makes for an interesting case study: Claude’s ability to write code was both what put us in this situation in the first place and how we were able to quickly build a high-quality, scalable system to deal with it. Growing our monorepo Before we explore what we built, we should acknowledge how unusual our workload is. Unsurprisingly, Anthropic uses Claude to write software far more than almost any other company, so we’re often the first to see where tools built for human scale start to strain. Source control is just one example of this. While we don’t expect many organizations to have these problems in the very near term, we suspect it won’t be too long before others who use AI coding tools experience these same pressure points, which is why we wanted to share what we built and what we learned. PCP: split the tokens, not the heads DCP: shard the KV cache too The deployment Results Making it all compose Try it Acknowledgements Notes Table of Contents TL;DR: Long agentic contexts push GLM-5.3 against two limits on H200s: KV cache memory and prefill speed. We address both on 16 H200s, split into one prefill node and one decode node: Prefill Context Parallelism (PCP) splits each prompt across GPUs by token instead of by head, which suits GLM-5.3's sparse attention far better than tensor parallelism. Decode Context Parallelism (DCP) shards the prefill engine's KV cache by token, so a 1M context fits on the prefill node. Hybrid HiSparse lets decode keep KV in host memory, so a 1M-token request fits. On AgentX, PCP8 × DCP8 prefill with Hybrid HiSparse decode gives 1.7–3.2× the per-user speed of a data-parallel deployment at the same throughput, and it is the only configuration we tested that serves 1M-token contexts. Serving long contexts in memory-constrained deployments Agentic workloads have long contexts that grow with every turn, which puts pressure on both GPU memory and prefill. On H200s, GLM-5.3's weights take up most of each GPU's memory, leaving little room for the KV cache of those long contexts. And because every turn adds more tool output and file contents to prefill, under load the prefill engines can become the bottleneck for the whole deployment. Part 1 showed how Hybrid HiSparse lets long contexts fit in an aggregated deployment on a single 8× H200 node. Prefill/decode disaggregation takes more than that. On the prefill node, we use PCP to speed up long prompts by parallelizing across the prompt's tokens. With MLA, however, this leaves every PCP rank holding a full copy of the KV cache, so we combine it with DCP to remove that replication. On the decode node, Hybrid HiSparse allows higher concurrency at long contexts. vLLM's new modular core ( Model Runner V2 ) makes composing all of this much easier. Why not TP or DP? More than 70 agent platforms, including ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and VS Code, have integrated Agent Skills since we published the standard in December 2025. Agent interoperability through simplicity A skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file that teaches an agent a specific task or domain, along with any scripts or reference material it needs. We developed skills while working on Claude Code. It handled general knowledge work well, but often lacked the procedural knowledge that real business tasks need. Within weeks of our October 2025 launch, developers published thousands of skills on GitHub and wrote loaders for Codex, Cursor, and OpenCode. We then published Agent Skills as an open standard, under its own GitHub organization and domain, so any agent could use it. So far, 1 million skills have been published and nearly 280 million installed. Donating Agent Skills to AAIF We’re committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral. Today, we are donating the standard to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation, which we co-founded with Block and OpenAI last year, and to which we donated the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The AAIF will provide a neutral home to the standard going forward, ensuring the community has a say in where Agent Skills go next. We are donating the Agent Skills name and logo, the GitHub organization, and the agentskills.io domain. You can continue to use the standard or contribute to it without joining the AAIF. Engineers from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and other companies will maintain the standard as individuals, with David Soria Parra and Mahesh Murag as Lead Maintainers. What comes next We’ve proposed starting with a roadmap covering versioned releases, a formal proposal process, and security guidance for people who write and install skills. It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens , and is released under the Apache 2.0 license. Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model. Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it. TL;DR 501B-parameter MoEs LLM with 23B active per token. 52 layers, 256 experts per MoE layer, 8 routed per token. Text in, text out with context window of 1M tokens.
